grammar.title: QUERER + infinitive — I want to
grammar.content:
The verb **querer** (to want) is one of the most common irregular verbs in Spanish. It follows a regular pattern in the present tense except for the first person singular.

Conjugation:
- yo **quiero** (I want)
- tú **quieres** (you want)
- él/ella **quiere** (he/she wants)
- nosotros **queremos** (we want)
- vosotros **queréis** (you all want)
- ellos **quieren** (they want)

To say 'I want to eat', you add the infinitive verb after 'quiero':
- Quiero **comer** una manzana. (I want to eat an apple.)
- Quiero **beber** agua. (I want to drink water.)
- Quiero **pagar** la cuenta. (I want to pay the bill.)

The infinitive never changes — only 'querer' is conjugated.
examples: Quiero comer una ensalada. (I want to eat a salad.)
Quiero beber un vaso de agua. (I want to drink a glass of water.)
Quiero pagar con tarjeta. (I want to pay with card.)
¿Quieres comprar pan? (Do you want to buy bread?)
grammar.note: Remember: 'querer' is stem-changing (e → ie). Only 'nosotros' and 'vosotros' keep the regular 'e'.

grammar.title: HAY vs ESTÁ — There is vs It is located
grammar.content:
Spanish has two ways to talk about presence and location:

**HAY** (from 'haber') — used for existence: 'there is' or 'there are'
- Hay pan en la tienda. (There is bread in the store.)
- Hay muchos clientes aquí. (There are many customers here.)

**ESTÁ** (from 'estar') — used for specific location of something known
- El pan está en la tienda. (The bread is in the store.)

Key difference:
- Use **hay** when introducing something new or unknown
- Use **está** when you already know what you're talking about and want to say where it is

Other common expressions:
- **Hay** que + infinitive = It is necessary to + ... (general obligation)
- Hay que pagar. (One must pay / You have to pay.)
examples: ¿Hay leche en la nevera? (Is there milk in the fridge?)
La leche está en la nevera. (The milk is in the fridge.)
¿Hay queso en la tienda? (Is there cheese in the store?)
El queso está en la estantería. (The cheese is on the shelf.)
grammar.note: In a shop context, use 'hay' to ask about availability and 'está' to point to where something is.

grammar.title: EL / LA vs UN / UNA — definite and indefinite articles
grammar.content:
Spanish nouns have gender, and articles must match:

**Definite articles** (the):
- **el** pan (m. sing.)
- **la** leche (f. sing.)
- **los** huevos (m. pl.)
- **las** manzanas (f. pl.)

**Indefinite articles** (a / some):
- **un** pan (m. sing.)
- **una** leche (f. sing.)
- **unos** huevos (m. pl.)
- **unas** manzanas (f. pl.)

In the supermarket, you can use either:
- Quiero **el** pan. = I want THE bread (specific)
- Quiero **un** pan. = I want A loaf of bread (any loaf)
- Quiero **dos** manzanas. = I want two apples (number replaces article)

Some foods are always singular, some are always plural:
- **la** pasta (always singular, even though it's many strands)
- **los** huevos (always plural in Spanish)
examples: Quiero una botella de agua. (I want a bottle of water.)
Necesito dos kilos de arroz. (I need two kilos of rice.)
El pan está fresco hoy. (The bread is fresh today.)
¿Tienes las manzanas rojas? (Do you have the red apples?)
grammar.note: Article agreement is essential — mismatching gender or number is one of the most common errors for English speakers.

tips: Spanish vowels are always short and clear — never diphthongized like in English. Practice: la manzana (not 'man-zuh-nuh').
The 'rr' is a strong trill. Place your tongue against the roof of your mouth and vibrate: el carretón, la carnicería.
'D' between vowels is soft, almost like an English 'th' or a gentle tap. Practice: la cuenta, el dinero.
'J' is a strong throat sound, like clearing your throat: la jalea, la jarra de agua.
'Ñ' is the 'ny' sound in 'canyon': la piña, el señor, mañana.

tricky_sounds.description: Strong trilled 'r', must vibrate the tongue against the roof of mouth
Soft 'd', almost like a gentle 'th' sound
In Spanish, 'b' and 'v' sound the same — a soft lip-close, not a 'v' as in English

dialogues.title: At the supermarket
dialogues.content:
Person A: ¿Qué necesitamos para la cena?
Person B: Necesitamos arroz, pollo, verduras y agua.
Person A: ¿Hay pan en la tienda?
Person B: No, pero hay una panadería cerca. ¿Quieres ir?
Person A: Sí, quiero comprar pan y queso.
